## Reproducible example

```r
mse_impl <- function(truth, estimate, case_weights = NULL) {
  mean((truth - estimate) ^ 2)
}

mse_vec <- function(truth, estimate, na_rm = TRUE, case_weights = NULL, ...) {
  check_numeric_metric(truth, estimate, case_weights)

  if (na_rm) {
    result <- yardstick_remove_missing(truth, estimate, case_weights)

    truth <- result$truth
    estimate <- result$estimate
    case_weights <- result$case_weights
  } else if (yardstick_any_missing(truth, estimate, case_weights)) {
    return(NA_real_)
  }

  mse_impl(truth, estimate, case_weights = case_weights)
}

mse <- function(data, ...) {
  UseMethod("mse")
}

mse <- new_numeric_metric(mse, direction = "minimize")

mse.data.frame <- function(data, truth, estimate, na_rm = TRUE, case_weights = NULL, ...) {

  numeric_metric_summarizer(
    name = "mse",
    fn = mse_vec,
    data = data,
    truth = !!enquo(truth),
    estimate = !!enquo(estimate),
    na_rm = na_rm,
    case_weights = !!enquo(case_weights)
  )
}

library(tidymodels)
data(ames)
```

title: `event_level` for `brier_class()`
description:
## The problem

Should `brier_class()` take `event_level` as a parameter? I feel like it is in the same realm as other `prob_metric`s and should allow `event_level` to be specified.

I'm happy to make a PR for this if y'all agree with me.

## Reproducible example

```r
library(yardstick)
data("two_class_example")
brier_class(two_class_example, truth, Class1)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 3
#>   .metric     .estimator .estimate
#>   <chr>       <chr>          <dbl>
#> 1 brier_class binary         0.106
## Should be different?
brier_class(two_class_example, truth, Class1, event_level = "second")
#> # A tibble: 1 × 3
#>   .metric     .estimator .estimate
#>   <chr>       <chr>          <dbl>
#> 1 brier_class binary         0.106

## Hand-crafted brier_class calcs
mse <- function(x, y) {
  mean((x - y)^2)
}

## Equivalent to brier_class(two_class_example, truth, Class1), as expected
mse(2 - as.integer(two_class_example$truth), two_class_example$Class1)
#> [1] 0.1056186
## Should be equivalent to brier_class(two_class_example, truth, Class1, event_level = "second")?
mse(as.integer(two_class_example$truth) - 1, two_class_example$Class1)
#> [1] 0.7402632
```

title: `<class_pred>` objects don't work everywhere
description:
``` r
library(yardstick)
#> For binary classification, the first factor level is assumed to be the event.
#> Use the argument `event_level = "second"` to alter this as needed.

df <- tibble::tibble(
  truth = probably::class_pred(factor(c("a", "b", "a", "c"))), 
  estimate = factor(c("a", "c", "a", "b"))
)

accuracy(df, truth, estimate)
#> Error in `dplyr::summarise()`:
#> ℹ In argument: `.estimate = fn(truth = truth, estimate = estimate, na_rm
#>   = na_rm)`.
#> Caused by error in `binary_checks()`:
#> ! `estimator` is binary, only two class `truth` factors are allowed. A factor with 3 levels was provided.

#> Backtrace:
#>      ▆
#>   1. ├─yardstick::accuracy(df, truth, estimate)
#>   2. ├─yardstick:::accuracy.data.frame(df, truth, estimate)
#>   3. │ └─yardstick::class_metric_summarizer(...)
#>   4. │   ├─dplyr::summarise(...)
#>   5. │   └─dplyr:::summarise.data.frame(...)
#>   6. │     └─dplyr:::summarise_cols(.data, dplyr_quosures(...))
#>   7. │       ├─base::withCallingHandlers(...)
#>   8. │       └─dplyr:::map(quosures, summarise_eval_one, mask = mask)
#>   9. │         └─base::lapply(.x, .f, ...)
#>  10. │           └─dplyr (local) FUN(X[[i]], ...)
#>  11. │             └─mask$eval_all_summarise(quo)
#>  12. │               └─dplyr (local) eval()
#>  13. └─yardstick (local) fn(truth = truth, estimate = estimate, na_rm = na_rm)
#>  14.   └─yardstick::metric_vec_template(...)
#>  15.     └─yardstick:::validate_truth_estimate_checks(...)
#>  16.       ├─yardstick:::validate_truth_estimate_types(truth, estimate, estimator)
#>  17.       └─yardstick:::validate_truth_estimate_types.factor(...)
#>  18.         ├─yardstick:::binary_checks(truth, estimate)
#>  19.         └─yardstick:::binary_checks.factor(truth, estimate)
#>  20.           └─rlang::abort(...)
```

I think `finalize_estimator()` is getting a `<class_pred>`, so its internal dispatch doesn't treat it like a factor. It might need to convert to a factor early before calling `finalize_estimator_internal()`

title: Can `validate_class()` print the function that called it?
description:
## The problem

Right now, if you hand a yardstick function the wrong class, you get an error from `validate_class()`:

``` r
yardstick::rmse_vec(c("a", "b"), c("3", "d"))
#> Error in `validate_class()`:
#> ! `truth` should be a numeric but a character was supplied.
```

<sup>Created on 2022-12-10 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

Similar errors come from passing the wrong type of object:

``` r
yardstick::rmse_vec(c(3, 2), matrix(2, 1))
#> Error in `validate_truth_estimate_types()`:
#> ! `estimate` should be a numeric vector, not a numeric matrix.
```

<sup>Created on 2022-12-10 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

I think this might be friendlier if (in this situation) the package printed `Error in 'rmse_vec()'`, using the original call.

title: Metrics calculated using `sf` objects return an unexpected geometry column
description:
## The problem

Hi all! I've got another odd behavior that might not be worth fixing: when `data` is an sf object, data.frame yardstick functions will return a fourth, unexpected `geometry` column containing (I think) the spatial union of input observations.

I _think_ you could work around this most of the time without adding a dependency via something like this to summarizers:

```r
if (!is.null(attr(out, "sf_column"))) out[attr(out, "sf_column")] <- NULL
```

But I'm not 100% sure that the attribute is supposed to be part of the "public" API (sf provides `sf::st_geometry()` as an accessor).

## Reproducible example

``` r
library(yardstick)
#> For binary classification, the first factor level is assumed to be the event.
#> Use the argument `event_level = "second"` to alter this as needed.

nc <- sf::st_read(system.file("shape/nc.shp", package = "sf"))
#> Reading layer `nc' from data source 
#>   `/home/mikemahoney218/R/x86_64-pc-linux-gnu-library/4.2/sf/shape/nc.shp' 
#>   using driver `ESRI Shapefile'
#> Simple feature collection with 100 features and 14 fields
#> Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: -84.32385 ymin: 33.88199 xmax: -75.45698 ymax: 36.58965
#> Geodetic CRS:  NAD27
rmse(nc, AREA, PERIMETER)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   .metric .estimator .estimate                                          geometry
#>   <chr>   <chr>          <dbl>                                <MULTIPOLYGON [°]>
#> 1 rmse    standard        1.61 (((-75.97629 36.51793, -75.97728 36.47802, -75.9…

# the output geometry appears to be the spatial union of observations
plot(rmse(nc, AREA, PERIMETER)$geometry)
```

title: Depreciation warning when using roc_curve
description:
< -- ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ -->

## The problem  

I get a warning message when attempting to use yardstick::roc_curve() while following the example code for tidymodels (https://www.tidymodels.org/start/recipes/):
Returning more (or less) than 1 row per `summarise()` group was deprecated in dplyr 1.1.0.


## Regex  

``` r
library(tidymodels)
library(nycflights13)

set.seed(123)

flight_data <- 
  flights %>% 
  mutate(
    arr_delay = ifelse(arr_delay >= 30, "late", "on_time"),
    arr_delay = factor(arr_delay),
    date = lubridate::as_date(time_hour)
  ) %>% 
  inner_join(weather, by = c("origin", "time_hour")) %>% 
  select(dep_time, flight, origin, dest, air_time, distance, 
         carrier, date, arr_delay, time_hour) %>% 
  na.omit() %>% 
  mutate_if(is.character, as.factor)

set.seed(222)
data_split <- initial_split(flight_data, prop = 3/4)

train_data <- training(data_split)
test_data  <- testing(data_split)

flights_rec <-
  recipe(arr_delay ~ ., data = train_data) %>%
  update_role(flight, time_hour, new_role = "ID") %>%
  step_date(date, features = c("dow", "month")) %>%
  step_holiday(date,
               holidays = timeDate::listHolidays("US"),
               keep_original_cols = FALSE) %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) %>%
  step_zv(all_predictors())

lr_mod <- logistic_reg() %>% 
  set_engine("glm")

flights_wflow <-
  workflow() %>%
  add_model(lr_mod) %>% 
  add_recipe(flights_rec)

flights_fit <- 
  flights_wflow %>% 
  fit(data = train_data)

flights_aug <- augment(flights_fit, test_data)

flights_aug %>% 
  roc_curve(truth = arr_delay, .pred_late) %>% 
  autoplot()
#> Warning: Returning more (or less) than 1 row per `summarise()` group was deprecated in
#> dplyr 1.1.0.
#> ℹ Please use `reframe()` instead.
#> ℹ When switching from `summarise()` to `reframe()`, remember that `reframe()`
#>   always returns an ungrouped data frame and adjust accordingly.
#> ℹ The deprecated feature was likely used in the yardstick package.
#>   Please report the issue at <https://github.com/tidymodels/yardstick/issues>.
#> This warning is displayed once every 8 hours.
#> Call `lifecycle::last_lifecycle_warnings()` to see where this warning was
#> generated.
```

title: initial survival metrics
description:
Let's table the ROC curves for now. There are some methodological issues to work out. 

I think that we should start with concordance for event time outcomes and Brier scores. 

Concordance is pretty straight-forward and there is [already some work on this](https://github.com/tidymodels/yardstick/tree/feature/survival-concordance).

For  Brier scores, I would start by implementing the binary and multi class versions first (for now, let's call that function `brier_class()`). The survival version(s) (say `brier_time()`?) would need an argument for the time to compute the probability. 
There was some previous work here too #18 and #202

Some open questions: 

* How do we include the time setting in the resulting data? 
* If someone specifies multiple time points, how would a user of the tune package specify one of them to optimize on? 
* Some Brier scores need to use weights based on the probability of a data point being censored. There are a lot of ways to do this but a simple KM curve, based on the training set, would do. How would we facilitate that? 
* Brier scores can also be decomposed in a few ways. We should think about doing that in specialized functions (as in #202).

title: `finalize_estimator` fails in metric summarizers when any column is named `name`
description:
## The problem

If any column of a data frame passed to `data` is named `name`, `finalize_estimator` will fail. This seems to be happening because `name` is being evaluated in the context of `data` inside of `summarise`:

https://github.com/tidymodels/yardstick/blob/3099e9973e0983ff134406d18920f82a8913dc32/R/template.R#L119-L120

Changing both of those lines to use `.env[["name"]]` seems to fix this behavior:

``` r
Orange2 <- Orange
Orange2$name <- Orange$circumference
library(rlang)
assignInNamespace(
  "numeric_metric_summarizer", 
  function(name,
           fn,
           data,
           truth,
           estimate,
           ...,
           na_rm = TRUE,
           case_weights = NULL,
           fn_options = list(),
           error_call = caller_env()) {
    rlang::check_dots_empty()
    
    truth <- enquo(truth)
    estimate <- enquo(estimate)
    case_weights <- enquo(case_weights)
    
    truth <- yardstick:::yardstick_eval_select(
      expr = truth,
      data = data,
      arg = "truth",
      error_call = error_call
    )
    estimate <- yardstick:::yardstick_eval_select(
      expr = estimate,
      data = data,
      arg = "estimate",
      error_call = error_call
    )
    
    if (!quo_is_null(case_weights)) {
      case_weights <- yardstick:::yardstick_eval_select(
        expr = case_weights,
        data = data,
        arg = "case_weights",
        error_call = error_call
      )
      
      case_weights <- expr(.data[[!!case_weights]])
    }
    
    out <- dplyr::summarise(
      data,
      .metric = .env[["name"]], # change 1
      .estimator = yardstick::finalize_estimator(
        .data[[truth]], 
        metric_class = .env[["name"]]), # change 2
      .estimate = fn(
        truth = .data[[truth]],
        estimate = .data[[estimate]],
        case_weights = !!case_weights,
        na_rm = na_rm,
        !!!fn_options
      )
    )
    
    dplyr::as_tibble(out)
  },
  "yardstick"
)
yardstick::rmse(Orange2, name, circumference)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 3
#>   .metric .estimator .estimate
#>   <chr>   <chr>          <dbl>
#> 1 rmse    standard           0
```

title: Same syntax, same arguments to conf_mat() and roc_auc() fails with roc_auc(), and inconsistent behavior in roc_auc() arguments
description:
## The problem

The function `conf_mat()` and `roc_auc()` have the same arguments (data, truth, estimate), and I expected them to behave similarly. However I was using character variables to refer to column names (like `target` and `prediction` to refer to the target and prediction variables). 

With `conf_mat()`, you can pass these variables as is, or use `get(variable)` or `!!variable`.

With `roc_auc()` however, the behavior is inconsistent: you can pass the variable to the `truth` argument using either `!!variable` or `get(variable)`, but not simply `variable`, in which case you get the error `truth should be a factor but a character was supplied.` Meanwhile, you can pass the variable to the `estimate` argument using either `!!variable` or as is `variable`, but not `get(variable)`, in which case you get the error `object 'prob' not found`.

The error message that accompanies `truth = variable` in particular gave me a headache, as it says truth should be a factor, and that's what I had.

So I see two oddities:

1. Inconsistent behavior between `conf_mat()` and `roc_auc()` when using variables to refer to variable names, even though they have the same format
2. Inconsistent behavior between the arguments of `roc_auc()` when using variables to refer to variable names

## Reproducible example

```r
library(tidymodels)
#> Warning: package 'tidymodels' was built under R version 4.1.1
#> Registered S3 method overwritten by 'tune':
#>   method                   from   
#>   required_pkgs.model_spec parsnip
#> Warning: package 'dials' was built under R version 4.1.1
#> Warning: package 'infer' was built under R version 4.1.1
#> Warning: package 'modeldata' was built under R version 4.1.1
#> Warning: package 'parsnip' was built under R version 4.1.1
#> Warning: package 'recipes' was built under R version 4.1.1
#> Warning: package 'rsample' was built under R version 4.1.1
#> Warning: package 'tune' was built under R version 4.1.1
#> Warning: package 'workflows' was built under R version 4.1.1
#> Warning: package 'workflowsets' was built under R version 4.1.1
#> Warning: package 'yardstick' was built under R version 4.1.1

# df
df<-data.frame(
  y=factor(c("A", "A", "B", "B", "B", "B")),
  pred=factor(c("A", "B", "A", "B", "B", "B")),
  prob=c(.88,.65,.7,.22,.44,.13)
)

# variables to refer to column names
target<-"y"
prediction<-"pred"
proba<-"prob"
```
```r
# evaluate model
# roc_auc: 
#   target can be !! or get, but not nothing
#   estimate can be !! or nothing, but not get
# conf_mat: 
#   everything works
```
```r
# with conf_mat
yardstick::conf_mat(df, truth=target, estimate=prediction)
#>           Truth
#> Prediction A B
#>          A 1 1
#>          B 1 3
yardstick::conf_mat(df, truth=get(target), estimate=prediction)
#>           Truth
#> Prediction A B
#>          A 1 1
#>          B 1 3
yardstick::conf_mat(df, truth=target, estimate=get(prediction))
#>           Truth
#> Prediction A B
#>          A 1 1
#>          B 1 3
yardstick::conf_mat(df, truth=!!target, estimate=prediction)
#>           Truth
#> Prediction A B
#>          A 1 1
#>          B 1 3
yardstick::conf_mat(df, truth=target, estimate=!!prediction)
#>           Truth
#> Prediction A B
#>          A 1 1
#>          B 1 3
```
```r
# with roc_auc
yardstick::roc_auc(df, truth=target, estimate=proba)
#> Note: Using an external vector in selections is ambiguous.
#> i Use `all_of(proba)` instead of `proba` to silence this message.
#> i See <https://tidyselect.r-lib.org/reference/faq-external-vector.html>.
#> This message is displayed once per session.
#> Error: Problem with `summarise()` column `.estimate`.
#> i `.estimate = metric_fn(...)`.
#> x `truth` should be a factor but a character was supplied.
yardstick::roc_auc(df, truth=get(target), estimate=proba)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 3
#>   .metric .estimator .estimate
#>   <chr>   <chr>          <dbl>
#> 1 roc_auc binary         0.875
yardstick::roc_auc(df, truth=target, estimate=get(proba))
#> Error: object 'prob' not found
yardstick::roc_auc(df, truth=target, estimate=!!proba)
#> Error: Problem with `summarise()` column `.estimate`.
#> i `.estimate = metric_fn(...)`.
#> x `truth` should be a factor but a character was supplied.
yardstick::roc_auc(df, truth=!!target, estimate=!!proba)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 3
#>   .metric .estimator .estimate
#>   <chr>   <chr>          <dbl>
#> 1 roc_auc binary         0.875
```

title: Remove uses of expect_error()
description:
There are some cases where `expect_error()` is called where it would be more benefical to use `expect_snapshot(error = TRUE)`

title: Consider using `reframe()` inside of `metric_summarizer()` rather than `summarise()`?
description:
## Feature

As of dplyr 1.1.0, `summarise` gives a warning when returning more than 1 row per group. As a result, `metric_summarizer()` now warns when metrics return more than one row for ungrouped data.frames:
``` r
library(yardstick)
#> For binary classification, the first factor level is assumed to be the event.
#> Use the argument `event_level = "second"` to alter this as needed.
library(rlang)

resid <- function(data, ...) {
  UseMethod("resid")
}

resid <- new_numeric_metric(resid, direction = "zero")

resid.data.frame <- function(data, truth, estimate, na_rm = TRUE, ...) {
  metric_summarizer(
    metric_nm = "residual",
    metric_fn = resid_vec,
    data = data,
    truth = !! enquo(truth),
    estimate = !! enquo(estimate),
    na_rm = na_rm,
    metric_fn_options = list(...)
  )
}

resid_vec <- function(truth, estimate, wt, na_rm = TRUE, ...) {
  
  resid_impl <- function(truth, estimate, ...) {
    truth - estimate
  }
  
  metric_vec_template(
    metric_impl = resid_impl,
    truth = truth,
    estimate = estimate,
    cls = "numeric",
    na_rm = na_rm,
    ...
  )
}

resid(data.frame(x = 1:5, y = 6:10), x, y)
#> Warning: Returning more (or less) than 1 row per `summarise()` group was deprecated in
#> dplyr 1.1.0.
#> ℹ Please use `reframe()` instead.
#> ℹ When switching from `summarise()` to `reframe()`, remember that `reframe()`
#>   always returns an ungrouped data frame and adjust accordingly.
#> ℹ The deprecated feature was likely used in the yardstick package.
#>   Please report the issue at <https://github.com/tidymodels/yardstick/issues>.
```

title: Why is error returned if the class is not in the levels?
description:
I'm wondering why it is not possible to calculate metrics of classification performance (e.g. Cohen's kappa or MCC) if the levels in the vectors differ. Currently, an error is returned. I think a fairly common situation is that the classifier has not learned to recognize all classes (i.e. it is underfitted).

```r
library("yardstick")
truth = factor(c("A", "A", "A", "B", "B", "C"))
predicted = factor(c("C", "C", "C", "A", "A", "A"))
kap_vec(truth, predicted)
mcc_vec(truth, predicted)
#> Error in `multiclass_checks()`:
#> ! `truth` and `estimate` levels must be equivalent.
#> `truth`: A, B, C
#> `estimate`: A, C
```

title: better description of probability column arguments.
description:
In our functions that use class probabilities (e.g. `roc_auc()`), we should be more explicit about the columns passed to `...`. 

For example, we should say that, for binary classification problems, this should be a single column that corresponds to the value of `yardstick_event_level()`. We should also say that the ordering of the columns should be the same as the factor levels (correct me if this is wrong).

title: Consider accepting `units` objects for numeric functions?
description:
## Feature

Hi all!

The [units](https://r-quantities.github.io/units/) package provides a class of vectors which contain a units attribute, which automatically handle unit conversion and tracking:

``` r
x <- units::set_units(1:5, "m")
y <- units::set_units(5:1, "ft")
x + y
#> Units: [m]
#> [1] 2.5240 3.2192 3.9144 4.6096 5.3048
```

These objects are becoming pretty prevalent throughout the spatial ecosystem (Edzer, who maintains sf, also wrote the units package) and are generally useful for dimensional analysis.

One feature of the package is that units objects do not subclass numeric vectors, but are instead their own units class:

```r
class(x)
#> [1] "units"
```

This prevents an easy type of error, where adding or subtracting a unitless value would return an object with questionable units.

```r
x + 2
#> Error in Ops.units(x, 2): both operands of the expression should be "units" objects
```

(For what it's worth, scaling factors work fine -- you can multiply or divide by a unitless vector).

Because these are not numeric vectors, they can't be used with yardstick functions right now:

```r
yardstick::rmse_vec(x, y)
#> Error in `validate_truth_estimate_types()`:
#> ! `truth` class `units` is unknown. `truth` must be a numeric or a factor.
```

I'm wondering if it would be possible to accept units objects as inputs to `validate_truth_estimate_types`:

```r
validate_truth_estimate_types.units <- function (truth, estimate, estimator) {
  if (!inherits(estimate, "units")) {
    cls <- class(estimate)[[1]]
    abort(paste0("`estimate` should be a units vector, not a `", 
                 cls, "`."))
  }
  if (is.matrix(estimate)) {
    abort(paste0("`estimate` should be a units vector, not a matrix."))
  }
  if (is.matrix(truth)) {
    abort(paste0("`truth` should be a units vector, not a units matrix."))
  }
}

# Note the correct units of the output, even though x and y are mismatched!
yardstick::rmse_vec(x, y)
#> 2.784732 [m]

# Compare to bare vectors:
yardstick::rmse_vec(1:5, 5:1)
#> [1] 2.828427
```

<sup>Created on 2022-12-10 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

description:
Dear tidymodels team,

The score is described here, along with 2-variable and 3-variable decompositions: [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brier_score](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brier_score)

All the best,

Karandeep

title: Requesting explicit event_level specification
description:
In addition to letting users specify `event_level` as "first" or "second" for example in `roc_curve()`, I think it would be helpful (and perhaps more intuitive) to let them specify `event_level` explicitly. This would reduce the likelihood of users getting confused about which level is first vs. second.

Setup:
```r
pred <- tibble::tibble(
  id = "train/test split", 
  .pred_A = c(.9, .8, .3, .4), 
  .pred_B = c(.1, .2, .7, .6), 
  .row = c(1, 2, 3, 4), 
  .pred_class = factor(c("A", "A", "B", "B")),
  class = factor(c("A", "A", "B", "B")), 
  .config = "Preprocessor1_Model1"
)
```

Current version:
```r
yardstick::roc_curve(pred, truth = class, .pred_B, event_level = "second")
```

Requested version:
```r
yardstick::roc_curve(pred, truth = class, .pred_B, event_level = "B")
```

title: Sensitivity and specificity switched?
description:
## The problem

I think that the specificity and sensitivity are not calculated correctly (or functions are mixed).

For example, with `1 FP`, `1 TN`, `1 TP` and `0 FN`, I would expect a specificity of `0.5`. However, `spec_vec` returns `1` and `sens_vec` returns `0.5`.

## Reproducible example

``` r
library(yardstick)
#> Warning: package 'yardstick' was built under R version 4.2.1
#> For binary classification, the first factor level is assumed to be the event.
#> Use the argument `event_level = "second"` to alter this as needed.

truth     <- as.factor(c(0, 0, 1)) 
predicted <- as.factor(c(1, 0, 1)) # 1 FP, 1 TN, 1 TP

spec_vec(truth, predicted) # Expected spec 0.5 but got 1
#> [1] 1
sens_vec(truth, predicted)
#> [1] 0.5
```

title: accuracy and ordering of factors -- perhaps linked to issue 162?
description:
Hi all,

I have a problem with accuracy -- it seems to depend on the ordering of factors.
There is a small reproducible example below.
Apologies for not using "reprex" -- I could not get the clipboard working as expected.


## The problem
1) The problem comes from the example at https://blogs.rstudio.com/ai/posts/2021-02-11-tabnet/
The strange factor levels "1.000000000000000000e+00" are how they appear in the example
2) I can't run the full example so I subsetted the data using 

```r
test1 <- read_csv(
  "HIGGS.csv.gz",
  col_names = c("class", ....),
  col_types = "fdddddddddddddddddddddddddddd",
  skip = 100000 ,
  n_max= 10    
  )
```
which leads to an error. However changing the skip
```r
skip = 100001
```
removes the error


## Reproducible example

```r
library(tidymodels)
p1<-structure(list(class = structure(c(1L, 2L, 1L), levels = c("0.000000000000000000e+00", 
"1.000000000000000000e+00"), class = "factor"), .pred_class = structure(c(2L, 
1L, 2L), levels = c("1.000000000000000000e+00", "0.000000000000000000e+00"
), class = "factor")), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", 
"tbl", "data.frame"))
yardstick::accuracy(p1, class, .pred_class)
yardstick::accuracy(p1, class, .pred_class,event_level = "first")
yardstick::accuracy(p1, class, .pred_class,event_level = "second")

p2<-structure(list(class = structure(c(1L, 2L, 2L), levels = c("1.000000000000000000e+00", 
"0.000000000000000000e+00"), class = "factor"), .pred_class = structure(c(1L, 
2L, 2L), levels = c("1.000000000000000000e+00", "0.000000000000000000e+00"
), class = "factor")), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", 
"tbl", "data.frame"))
yardstick::accuracy(p2, class, .pred_class)
```

p1 gives an error. Setting event_level does not fix it. p2 works as expected.
The error is
```r
Error in `dplyr::summarise()`:
! Problem while computing `.estimate = metric_fn(truth = class, estimate
  = .pred_class, na_rm = na_rm)`.
Caused by error in `binary_checks()`:
! `truth` and `estimate` levels must be equivalent.
`truth`: 0.000000000000000000e+00, 1.000000000000000000e+00
`estimate`: 1.000000000000000000e+00, 0.000000000000000000e+00
Run `rlang::last_error()` to see where the error occurred.
```

title: f_meas cannot be calculated
description:
I try to flag `1` as the positive class in this example;


```
library(tidymodels)
library(dplyr)

set.seed(1)


iris2 <- iris %>%
mutate(dummy_class = as.factor(sample(0:1,size = n(),replace =T,prob = c(0.95,0.05)))) 


resampl <- vfold_cv(iris2,v = 3,strata = dummy_class)

metrics <- metric_set(accuracy,f_meas)

mod <- rand_forest() %>%
set_engine('ranger') %>%
set_mode('classification')

ctrl <- control_resamples(verbose = T,event_level = "second")


wf <- workflow() %>%
add_formula(dummy_class ~ Sepal.Width + Petal.Length) %>%
add_model(mod)

fit_rsmpl <- wf %>% fit_resamples(resamples = resampl,metrics = metrics,control = ctrl)
```

it works well when `0` is positive class but in the example above, I get this messages for each fold and f_meas is not calculated;

`While computing binary 'precision()', no predicted events were detected (i.e.'true_positive + false_positive = 0'). Precision is undefined in this case, and'NA' will be returned. Note that 2 true event(s) actually occured for the problematic event level, '1'.
`

other metrics work also.

```

  <chr>    <chr>       <dbl> <int>   <dbl> <chr>               
1 accuracy binary       0.96     3  0.0115 Preprocessor1_Model1

```

Thanks in advance

title: Idea for documenting metric implementation details
description:
At some point, we need to document the details of all of the metrics. I suggest a vignette, rather than trying to shove it inside the Rd with it's crappy latex parser. Luckily, pkgdown sites load the math beautifully. If we put it all in the vignette, and name each section in the vignette using the name of the function, then we can probably generate all of the links dynamically using a Rd template and using a template parameter. That way, we can link to the pkgdown section directly from the Rd.

Probably looks like:

```
https://tidymodels.github.io/yardstick/articles/metric-implementation.html#rmse
```

where that last `rmse` bit will be dynamic based on a template param. And that link lives in an `Implementation` section in the Rd of `rmse()`

title: unexpected behavior: truth and estimate columns not used as defaults in rsq()
description:
## The problem

From the help file to `rsq()` (and more generally `metrics()`), I expected to be able to supply a `data.frame` with columns `truth` and `estimate`, and have `rsq()` use those columns by default. 

I concluded this from the argument description for `data`:

```
data	A data.frame containing the `truth` and `estimate` columns.
```

However, when I do so, it gives me an error. 

## Reproducible example

```r
df <- data.frame(truth = c(1, 2, 3, 4), estimate = c(1, 1, 3, 4))

yardstick::rsq(df)
```

gives me:
```
Error in `validate_not_missing()`:
! `truth` is missing and must be supplied.
Backtrace:
 1. yardstick::rsq(df)
 2. yardstick:::rsq.data.frame(df)
 3. yardstick::metric_summarizer(...)
 4. yardstick:::validate_not_missing(truth, "truth")
 Error in validate_not_missing(truth, "truth") :
```

Am i misreading the helpfile? If so, would it make sense to have `rsq()` look for columns named `truth` and `estimate` as defaults?

title: `mape()` division by zero issues
description:
``` r
library(yardstick)
#> For binary classification, the first factor level is assumed to be the event.

mape_vec(truth = c(1, 0, 2), estimate = c(.9, .1, 2.1))
#> [1] Inf

mape_vec(truth = c(1, .Machine$double.eps, 2), estimate = c(.9, 0, 2.1))
#> [1] 38.33333
```

<sup>Created on 2022-04-01 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

title: `j_index()` needs to use `weighted.mean(na.rm = TRUE)` for multi class
description:
In #118 we changed `sens()`, `spec()`, `recall()`, and `precision()` to throw warnings when the denom is `0` and remove those cases from the weighted average when doing a multiclass average.

We also updated `f_meas()` to do this too, which is a hybrid of `precision()` and `recall()`.

But we didn't update `j_index()`, a hybrid of `sens()` and `spec()`

``` r
library(yardstick)
#> For binary classification, the first factor level is assumed to be the event.
#> Use the argument `event_level = "second"` to alter this as needed.

levels <- c("a", "b", "c", "d")

# When `d` is the event we get sens      = 0.5 = (tp = 1, fn = 1)
# When `a` is the event we get sens      = 1   = (tp = 1, fn = 0)
# When `b` is the event we get a warning = NA  = (tp = 0, fn = 0)
# When `c` is the event we get a warning = NA  = (tp = 0, fn = 0)
truth    <- factor(c("a", "d", "d"), levels = levels)
estimate <- factor(c("a", "d", "c"), levels = levels)

# Removes NAs when doing weighted average
sens_vec(truth, estimate)
#> Warning: While computing multiclass `sens()`, some levels had no true events (i.e. `true_positive + false_negative = 0`). 
#> Sensitivity is undefined in this case, and those levels will be removed from the averaged result.
#> Note that the following number of predicted events actually occured for each problematic event level:
#> 'b': 0
#> 'c': 1
#> [1] 0.75

# Doesn't do `na.rm = TRUE`
j_index_vec(truth, estimate)
#> Warning: While computing multiclass `recall()`, some levels had no true events (i.e. `true_positive + false_negative = 0`). 
#> Recall is undefined in this case, and those levels will be removed from the averaged result.
#> Note that the following number of predicted events actually occured for each problematic event level:
#> 'b': 0
#> 'c': 1
#> [1] NA

# Mix of recall/precision
f_meas_vec(truth, estimate)
#> Warning: While computing multiclass `precision()`, some levels had no predicted events (i.e. `true_positive + false_positive = 0`). 
#> Precision is undefined in this case, and those levels will be removed from the averaged result.
#> Note that the following number of true events actually occured for each problematic event level:
#> 'b': 0
#> Warning: While computing multiclass `recall()`, some levels had no true events (i.e. `true_positive + false_negative = 0`). 
#> Recall is undefined in this case, and those levels will be removed from the averaged result.
#> Note that the following number of predicted events actually occured for each problematic event level:
#> 'b': 0
#> 'c': 1
#> [1] 0.8333333
```

title: Mean Square Error metric
description:
Both, the yardstick vignette [Custom metric](https://yardstick.tidymodels.org/articles/custom-metrics.html) and the [Custom performance metrics](https://www.tidymodels.org/learn/develop/metrics/) article on [tidymodels](https://www.tidymodels.org/) discuss the Mean Square Error metric, `mse()`, but this is **not** a metric implemented in yardstick. This seems a bit curious.

What is implemented is the root mean squared error `rmse()` which is in the same units as the original data, but `mse()` is still wildly used. Wouldn´t be a good idea to implement `mse()` as a verb?

`mse()` is implemented in [modelr](https://modelr.tidyverse.org/reference/model-quality.html) with a different syntaxt that is used in [yardstick](https://yardstick.tidymodels.org/reference/rmse.html).

title: Do yardstick's `roc_au*` functions only work with probabilities and not ranks?
description:
## The problem
Do yardstick's `roc_au*` functions only work with probabilities and not ranks?
## Reproducible example
Using [important_words_cases.csv](https://github.com/tidymodels/yardstick/files/7808401/important_words_cases.csv), I find an AUC of 0.8216 both manually calculating the AUC, as seen [here](https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/145566/how-to-calculate-area-under-the-curve-auc-or-the-c-statistic-by-hand), and with `pROC::roc()`. When I calculate the AUC with yardstick, I either receive errors or an AUC of 0.1784.
```r
library(readr)

df <- read_csv("important_words_cases.csv")

truestat <- df$important_cases         # Outcomes from test data

testres <- df$important_words        # Ranks/probabilities estimated on test data

tab <- as.matrix(table(truestat, testres))    # Combination of outcomes and ranks/probabilities

tot <- colSums(tab)                           # Number with each test result
truepos <- unname(rev(cumsum(rev(tab[2,]))))  # Number of true positives
falsepos <- unname(rev(cumsum(rev(tab[1,])))) # Number of false positives
totpos <- sum(tab[2,])                        # The total number of positives
totneg <- sum(tab[1,])                        # The total number of negatives
sens <- truepos/totpos                        # Sensitivity (fraction of true positives)
omspec <- falsepos/totneg                     # 1 − specificity (fraction of false positives)

sens <- c(sens,0)                             # Begin at zero on y-axis
omspec <- c(omspec,0)                         # Begin at zero on x-axis

plot(omspec, sens, type="b", xlim=c(0,1), ylim=c(0,1), lwd=2,
     xlab="1 − specificity", ylab="Sensitivity") #plot of the ROC curve
grid()
abline(0,1, col="red", lty=2)

height <- (sens[-1]+sens[-length(sens)])/2    # midway between the two points for the height
width <- -diff(omspec)                        # diff is the difference between two points for the width
sum(height*width)                             # This is area, which gives the ROC-AUC

plot(jitter(truestat,.2), jitter(testres,.8), las=1,
     xlab="True case status", ylab="important words") # jitter plot of ranks/probabilities and true case status for sanity check on AUC

pROC::roc(data = df, response = important_cases, predictor = important_words)

yardstick::roc_aunp_vec(truth = as.factor(df$important_cases), estimate = df$important_words)

yardstick::roc_aunu_vec(truth = as.factor(df$important_cases), estimate = df$important_words)

yardstick::roc_auc_vec(truth = as.factor(df$important_cases), estimate = df$important_words)

yardstick::roc_auc(df, truth = as.factor(important_cases), estimate = important_words)
```
Here is the ROC curve:

title: Access underlying data of `autoplot()` objects
description:
The `autoplot()` functions are great out of the box for quick insights, but I wish there was a way to access the underlying data used to generate said plots. For example the `autoplot.conf_mat()` does the data prep and the plotting. If users could access the underlying data we could generate custom visualizations.

The data prep isn't trivial either especially for the "mosaic" type plots. 

https://github.com/tidymodels/yardstick/blob/5f1068ff8bdd402416996da35352526a80c4c966/R/conf_mat.R#L343-L379

It would be great if there was an optional arg to just return the data or even a separate user facing function. Hadley describes this as a best practice [here](https://r-pkgs.org/r.html#isolate-side-effects).

> 7.5.3 Isolate side effects
Creating plots and printing output to the console are two other ways of affecting the global R environment. Often you can’t avoid these (because they’re important!) but it’s good practice to isolate them in functions that only produce output. This also makes it easier for other people to repurpose your work for new uses. ***For example, if you separate data preparation and plotting into two functions, others can use your data prep work (which is often the hardest part!) to create new visualisations***.

Let me know what your opinions are. I know there's a bunch of different `autoplot()` functions so any change probably warrants further discussion. Thank you!

title: Evaluating prediction intervals?
description:
What is guidance on best-practices for evaluating prediction intervals with {tidymodels}? 

Example for measuring coverage on out-of-sample data (the rate at which records are observed to fall within their intervals, i.e. to check whether a 95% prediction interval has 95% coverage):

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)

set.seed(1)
split <- initial_split(mpg)
train <- training(split)
test <- testing(split)

lm_mod <- linear_reg() %>% 
  set_engine("lm") %>% 
  fit(hwy ~ displ + cty, data = train)

pred_intervals <- preds_interval <- predict(lm_mod, test, type = "pred_int") %>% 
  bind_cols(test)

coverage <- function(df, truth, lower, upper){
  df %>% 
    mutate(.covered = {{ truth }} >= {{ lower }} & {{ truth }} <= {{ upper }}) %>% 
    summarise(coverage = sum(.covered) / n())
}

pred_intervals %>% 
  coverage(truth = hwy, lower = .pred_lower, upper = .pred_upper)
```
It seems it would be *possible* to set-up a [custom metric](https://yardstick.tidymodels.org/articles/custom-metrics.html) to do this within {yardstick} but would have to use `estimate` argument, e.g. so something like `coverage(truth = hwy, estimate = c(.pred_lower, .pred_upper))`.

But this feels a bit awkward as {yardstick} is meant to evaluate individual or multiple `estimate`(s) -- not intervals (though could perhaps use `yardstick` to measure after calculating `.covered`) or things pertaining to the distributions associated with the estimates.

Hence, am curious how would recommend evaluating prediction intervals (preferably in a way that carries with it the [benefits](https://yardstick.tidymodels.org/articles/custom-metrics.html#custom-metrics) with {yardstick})? Or if an extension package on {yardstick} makes sense...

(This issue stems from Rstudio Community [thread](https://community.rstudio.com/t/prediction-intervals-with-tidymodels-best-practices/82594/21) and Mara's encouragement to open an issue to move discussion to github.)

title: Discussion: Classification vs. class probability metrics
description:
Hi,

I love the `yardstick` package but I always find myself trying to use both classification and class probability metrics in a single metric set for `workflows` or `workflowsets`, and always run into the issue that they don't accept the same type of input for `estimate`. I always feel like it should _"just work"_. This is probably because I regularly use `torchmetrics`, which allows you to use any of the classification metrics for the same inputs. The thresholding to form discrete levels is handled by the metric function itself, so it makes these classification functions easy to work with because they all take the same inputs, the difference is just how the computations go on behind the scenes. I like this approach because classification metrics are sort of a special case of class probability metrics where some thresholding has been done to the `estimate`. A default `threshold` of 0.5 is a sensible default, I think.

Is there any room in the `yardstick` world to either modify the classification metrics to be more general in that they can optionally accept the same `estimate` type as the class probability metrics, and add a `threshold` argument? To avoid issues with backwards compatibility, perhaps the `estimate` argument for classification metrics could accept either a factor (the current behaviour), or numeric/probability which gets thresholded and factored as processing step.

For a simple use case, when you have a binary outcome and fit a model that spits out probabilities (e.g. logistic regression), I think it would be nice to be able to get `roc_auc`, `pr_auc`, `sensitivity`,  `specificity`, etc. in a metric set with less friction.

`torchmetrics`, for reference (using specificity as an example): https://torchmetrics.readthedocs.io/en/latest/references/functional.html#specificity-func

title: Using a `metric_set` with `tune_grid()` or `fit_resamples()`
description:
Hi,

Every time I come up against this issue I can never remember how to tackle it: **How do you pass `event_level = "second"` to a `metric_set()` when using `tune_grid()` or `fit_resamples()`?**

When you, as the user, are calling the `metric_set()` directly, you pass it in as an argument, but there doesn't seem to be a way to do it when you aren't the one calling the metric set, such as when it is called internally by `tune_grid()` or `fit_resamples()`. Am I missing something?

``` r
library(tidymodels)

mtcars$vs <- factor(mtcars$vs)

ms <- metric_set(roc_auc)

## Manually pass event_level
ms(mtcars, truth = vs, mpg, event_level = "second")
#> # A tibble: 1 x 3
#>   .metric .estimator .estimate
#>   <chr>   <chr>          <dbl>
#> 1 roc_auc binary         0.911

## With tune_grid() or fit_resamples()
rs <- bootstraps(mtcars, times = 5)

workflow() %>% 
  add_model(logistic_reg() %>% set_engine("glm")) %>% 
  add_formula(vs ~ mpg) %>% 
  fit_resamples(
    resamples = rs,
    metrics = ms
  )
#> # Resampling results
#> # Bootstrap sampling 
#> # A tibble: 5 x 4
#>   splits          id         .metrics         .notes          
#>   <list>          <chr>      <list>           <list>          
#> 1 <split [32/12]> Bootstrap1 <tibble [1 × 4]> <tibble [0 × 1]>
#> 2 <split [32/10]> Bootstrap2 <tibble [1 × 4]> <tibble [0 × 1]>
#> 3 <split [32/13]> Bootstrap3 <tibble [1 × 4]> <tibble [0 × 1]>
#> 4 <split [32/10]> Bootstrap4 <tibble [1 × 4]> <tibble [0 × 1]>
#> 5 <split [32/16]> Bootstrap5 <tibble [1 × 4]> <tibble [0 × 1]>
```

It *feels* like you should be able to do this when creating the `metric_set`:
```r
ms <- metric_set(roc_auc, event_level = "second")
```
Where unnamed arguments are taken to be metric functions, while named arguments are passed along to the metric functions when they are called as part of the metric set. What do you think?

Similar to `metric_tweak()`, `data`, `truth`, and `estimate` would be protected, but any other optional arguments can be passed as named arguments to `metric_set()`.

title: pr_auc give unintuitive value for constant prediction
description:
When logistic regression model predicts 1 constant value (eg a model with an intercept only ie predict the sample probability always), the pr_auc function does not give intuitive value. It is likely due to the use of trapezoidal rule for calculating the area under curve. Maybe have to ignore the area under the curve to the left of the smallest predicted value? 

I don't know if it is 'wrong' but at least currently it is not intuitive. For example, a glmnet might give unintuitively high pr_auc as the L1 penalty goes really high to the point of 1 intercept term only, due to this problem with pr_auc. 

The pr_curve() autoplot() also seems non intuitive due to the linear interpolation making the pr curve look a lot better than it should be. 



```
library(tidyverse)

N <- 10000
p <- 0.01
set.seed(100)

df <- tibble(truth_factor = factor(sample(c('TRUE', 'FALSE'), N, replace = TRUE, prob = c(p, 1-p)), levels = c('TRUE', 'FALSE'))) %>%
  mutate(truth_num = if_else(truth_factor == 'TRUE', 1, 0)) %>%
  mutate(pred_const = 0.01) %>%
  mutate(pred_const2 = if_else(row_number() < n()/2, 0, 1)) %>%
  mutate(pred_rand = runif(n()))

yardstick::pr_auc(df, truth = truth_factor, pred_rand)$.estimate     # 0.02377628 ok
MLmetrics::PRAUC(df$pred_rand, df$truth_num)                         # 0.01515559
yardstick::pr_curve(df, truth = truth_factor, pred_rand) %>% autoplot()

yardstick::pr_auc(df, truth = truth_factor, pred_const)$.estimate    # 0.5058 wrong
MLmetrics::PRAUC(df$pred_const, df$truth_num)                        # 0
yardstick::pr_curve(df, truth = truth_factor, pred_const) %>% autoplot()

yardstick::pr_auc(df, truth = truth_factor, pred_const2)$.estimate    # 0.2194559 still wrong
MLmetrics::PRAUC(df$pred_const2, df$truth_num)                        # 0.006179606
yardstick::pr_curve(df, truth = truth_factor, pred_const2) %>% autoplot()


```

title: Support for `metric_set(list_of_funcs)` or `do.call(metric_set, list)`
description:
I really like tidymodels. Thanks for all the hard work.

Would it be possible to create a metric_set object from a list of metric functions? It would be great if `metric_set()` could detect when it's passed a list argument and work automatically like `dplyr::bind_rows()`.

I don't know if it would be any easier to implement, but one alternative is to allow the usual `do.call()`. Right now, using `do.call()` incorrectly fills in the `metric` column, which causes problems for functions like `show_best()`.

``` r
library(tune)
suppressMessages(library(yardstick))

metric_list <- c(f_meas, roc_auc)
mset_from_dots <- metric_set(f_meas, roc_auc)
mset_from_list <- do.call(metric_set, metric_list)

mset_from_dots
#>    metric        class direction
#> 1  f_meas class_metric  maximize
#> 2 roc_auc  prob_metric  maximize

mset_from_list
#>       metric        class direction
#> 1 <clss_mtr> class_metric  maximize
#> 2 <prb_mtrc>  prob_metric  maximize
```

title: Add KS metric for model evaulation
description:
I like to suggest adding KS metric for model performance evaluation.  I have seen KS used in the financial industry very much as the only metric for model evaluation for binary classification problems.  MLmetrics package can calculate this metric.

Here is a reproducible example on the metric:

```r
df <- cbind.data.frame(dep_var = sample(c(0,1), size = 100, replace = TRUE),
                       x1 = rnorm(100), x2 = rnorm(100))

library(caret)
model <- caret::train(as.factor(dep_var) ~., 
                      data = df, 
                      method = 'glm',
                      family="binomial")

library(MLmetrics)
MLmetrics::KS_Stat(predict(model, df[,c('x1','x2')],
                          type = 'prob')[,2],df$dep_var)
```

title: metric_set: Ability to alter arguments with purrr::partial
description:
## Problem

I have a `yardstick::metric_set()` that I use all the time for forecasting with `modeltime`. 

```
yardstick::metric_set(
        mae,
        mape,
        mase,
        smape,
        rmse,
        rsq
    )
```

The `mase` function has a parameter `m = 1` that we often want to change based on seasonality in the data (e.g. m = 12 for monthly data). 

My thought was to allow `purrr::partial()` to do this work for us. Something like this:

```
yardstick::metric_set(
    mae,
    mape,
    partial(mase, m = 12),
    smape,
    rmse,
    rsq
)
```

## Reprex

``` r
library(yardstick)
#> For binary classification, the first factor level is assumed to be the event.
#> Use the argument `event_level = "second"` to alter this as needed.
library(tibble)
library(purrr)

fake_data <- tibble(
    val1 = c(1:12, 2*1:12), 
    val2 = c(1 + 1:12, 2*1:12 - 1)
)

# OK
yardstick::metric_set(
    mae,
    mape,
    mase,
    smape,
    rmse,
    rsq
)
#>   metric          class direction
#> 1    mae numeric_metric  minimize
#> 2   mape numeric_metric  minimize
#> 3   mase numeric_metric  minimize
#> 4  smape numeric_metric  minimize
#> 5   rmse numeric_metric  minimize
#> 6    rsq numeric_metric  maximize

partial(mase, m = 1)(fake_data, val1, val2)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 3
#>   .metric .estimator .estimate
#>   <chr>   <chr>          <dbl>
#> 1 mase    standard       0.535
partial(mase, m = 12)(fake_data, val1, val2)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 3
#>   .metric .estimator .estimate
#>   <chr>   <chr>          <dbl>
#> 1 mase    standard       0.154

# Now if I want to change `mase(m = 12)`
# Error:
yardstick::metric_set(
    mae,
    mape,
    partial(mase, m = 12),
    smape,
    rmse,
    rsq
)
#> Error: 
#> The combination of metric functions must be:
#> - only numeric metrics
#> - a mix of class metrics and class probability metrics
#> 
#> The following metric function types are being mixed:
#> - numeric (mae, mape, smape, rmse, rsq)
#> - purrr_other_partial (partial(mase, m = 12))
```

title: Set autoplot.conf_mat() axis names based on the input conf_mat()$table dimnames
description:
When plotting a confusion matrix with custom names, 

```
foo <- factor(sample(1:5, 100, replace = T))
bar <- factor(sample(1:5, 100, replace = T))
df <- data.frame(foo, bar)
conf <- yardstick::conf_mat(df, foo, bar, dnn = c("custom", "names"))
conf
    names
custom 1 2 3 4 5
     1 6 7 7 2 3
     2 3 8 3 4 4
     3 2 4 5 5 4
     4 6 3 5 2 3
     5 4 3 4 0 3
```

I noticed that the autoplot method does not take the dimention names from the table. Instead the axis names are hardcoded to "Prediction" and "Truth".

autoplot(conf)
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/64198462/98125413-be43e800-1eb4-11eb-86f5-cb2a222bbd47.png)

I think it make sense to let the user be able to define custom axis names, either as part of autoplot, or as the title suggests, by letting autoplot take the names defined in the confusion matrix. 

The background is: I am comparing two competing classification outputs, so instead of "Prediction"/"Truth" , something like "Classification foo"/"Classification bar" makes more sense.

Would you be willing to merge a PR that allows for optional passing of lower and/or upper boundary for the AUC computation? I guess the best way to handle normalization is to renormalize by the width of the actual integration range?

title: ppv is incorrectly calculated when sensitivity is NA
description:
Consider the following example:

```
library(yardstick)
library(tidyverse)

df = tibble(
    truth = FALSE, 
    est = TRUE
) %>% mutate_all(factor, levels=c("TRUE", "FALSE"))

df
# A tibble: 1 x 2
  truth est  
  <fct> <fct>
1 FALSE TRUE 

df %>% ppv(truth, est)
# A tibble: 1 x 3
  .metric .estimator .estimate
  <chr>   <chr>          <dbl>
1 ppv     binary            NA
```

The ppv comes out as `NA` when it should clearly be 0/1 = 0. The problem is that a formula involving specificity and sensitivity is used in the code to calculate ppv. In this example, the sensitivity is `NA`, which corrupts the calculation. 

The formula that is used is useful in settings with biased case-control sampling, but otherwise should not be used. If no prevalence is provided, the calculation should be something like `mean(truth[est=="TRUE"]=="TRUE")`.

description:
We need to be able to compute these out-of-sample statistics in `yardstick`. 

We could have `weibull_log_loss()`, `lognormal_log_loss()`, and so on. 

Alternatively, we could also use `censored_log_loss(distribution = "family name")` in one function. 

The latter approach would probably be better since we will need to have the same metric name so that different tuning parameters can be compared. This, in turn, raises the question about how `tune` will collect the given out-of-sample predictions to the appropriate distribution. That is more of an issue/question for `tune` but is worth mentioning here.

title: Make it more visible that the default class is the first level
description:
Hi Max,

Thanks for making this useful package! I have a suggestion:

Taking the first level of response as the class of interest can lead to problems since most (in my limited experience) binary problems use the {0,1} or {-1,1} encoding for the response variable where `1` denotes the class of interest. It should be mentioned in the `README.md` just so that people are aware that  by default it ends up taking class 0 as the class of interest, and they can use the `options(yardstick.event_first = FALSE)` to disable this behaviour.

An example of the possible errors it can lead to are the precision/recall numbers [in this article.](http://www.business-science.io/business/2017/11/28/customer_churn_analysis_keras.html)

Perhaps it might be better to set the default value for `yardstick.event_first` to `FALSE` and allow the user to override it to `TRUE` in case their response uses the lower level value to denote the class of interest?

Regards,

Akshat

title: add pr_curve function
description:
So there's both `roc_auc` and `pr_auc`, and `roc_curve`, but no `pr_curve`; would it make sense to add one?

Pretty sure I could implement this if desired; made a rough version for a project recently:

```r
# loosely patterned after yardstick::roc_curve
pr_curve <- function(data, truth, prob) {
  
  truth <- enquo(truth)
  prob  <- enquo(prob)
  
  levs <- levels(pull(data, !!truth))
  
  roc_curve(data, !!truth, !!prob) %>%
    mutate(precision = map_dbl(
      threshold,
      ~data %>%
        mutate(predicted = factor(if_else(!!prob > .x, "yes", "no"), levels = levs)) %>%
        precision(!!truth, predicted)
    )) %>%
    select(threshold, recall = sensitivity, precision)
}
```

That needs to be further abstracted, but it's a start.

title: Facilitate per-group metrics
description:
I often find myself having a large tibble of predictions from different models. If I want to use `yardstick` to compute metrics per-model, the experience is a bit rough:

``` r
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
library(yardstick)
#> Loading required package: broom
#> For binary classification, the first factor level is assumed to be the event.
#> Set the global option `yardstick.event_first` to `FALSE` to change this.

tbl <- tibble(
  model_id  = rep(1:2, each = 3),
  actual    = rep(1:3, 2),
  predicted = c(1, 1, 3, 3, 2, 1)
) %>%
  mutate_at(vars(-model_id), factor, levels = 1:3)

# no grouping
accuracy(tbl, actual, predicted)
#> [1] 0.5

# grouping ignored
tbl %>%
  group_by(model_id) %>%
  accuracy(actual, predicted)
#> [1] 0.5

# works but ugly
tbl %>%
  group_by(model_id) %>%
  do(log_loss = accuracy(., actual, predicted)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(log_loss = rlang::flatten_dbl(log_loss))
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>   model_id log_loss
#>      <int>    <dbl>
#> 1        1    0.667
#> 2        2    0.333


# example implementation
accuracy.grouped_df <- function(tbl, actual, predicted, out = "accuracy") {
  actual <- enquo(actual)
  predicted <- enquo(predicted)
  
  # wouldn't use MLmetrics in actual implementation
  summarize(tbl, !!out := MLmetrics::Accuracy(predicted, actual))
}

# works now!
tbl %>%
  group_by(model_id) %>%
  accuracy(actual, predicted)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>   model_id accuracy
#>      <int>    <dbl>
#> 1        1    0.667
#> 2        2    0.333
```

title: Metrics in confusion matrix consistent with caret?

``` r
                method = "glm", family = "binomial")

library(yardstick)

        mutate(`Logistic regression` = predict(glmfit, testing))

conf1 <- conf_mat(testing_results, truth = Class, estimate = `Logistic regression`)
```

title: Pretty conf_mat in Rmarkdown
description:
I love how the `conf_mat` output looks in my console, and would like to make it look similarly nice in an Rmarkdown document. The output seems hard to coerce to a data.frame/tibble to then be `kable`'d, and I had high hopes for `results='asis'` but that squashes the bulk of the content to a single line.

How could we add some support for making these things look nice in knitted output? What's the right path here?

#### _Minimal_ Reproducible Dataset:

If you are not using a data set in a package then use e.g. `dput()` to give us something that can be put in R immediately, e.g. 

```r
dput(head(iris,4))
```

Without a dataset, there usually isn't much that we can do to help. 

If your data frame has a factor with many levels, the `dput` output can be unwieldy because it will still list all the possible factor levels even if they aren't present in the the subset of your data. To solve this issue, you can use the `droplevels()` function. Notice below how species is a factor with only one level: `dput(droplevels(head(iris, 4)))`.

```r
library(yardstick)

data("hpc_cv")
hpc_cv %>%
  filter(Resample == "Fold01") %>%
  conf_mat(obs, pred)
```

title: Consider exporting metric_summarizer() and metric_vec_template()
description:
When working on the `gain_capture()` metric in `probably`, I found myself wanting the infrastructure that I had built in `yardstick` to consistently create metrics. All that would need to be exported is `metric_summarizer()` for running the metric on (potentially grouped) data frames, and `metric_vec_template()` for running the actual metric implementation on vectors.

Then others could follow our implementation pattern to add their own metrics in their own packages. It would automatically put their metric output in the right form so their metrics would work with `metric_set()`.

Would need to document this pattern so others would know how to use it.

title: Huber Loss
description:
This is a numeric metric.

I like this metric as a mix of MSE and MAE. Apparently used in robust regression? 
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huber_loss

It looks like the implementation would be:


![equation](https://latex.codecogs.com/gif.latex?L_%7B%5Cdelta%7D%28y_i%2C%20%5Chat%7By%7D_i%29%20%3D%20%5Cbegin%7Bcases%7D%20%5Cfrac%7B1%7D%7B2%7D%7B%28y_i%20-%20%5Chat%7By%7D_i%29%5E2%7D%20%26%20%5Ctext%7Bfor%20%7D%20%7Cy_i%20-%20%5Chat%7By%7D_i%7C%20%5Cle%20%5Cdelta%2C%20%5C%5C%20%5Cdelta%20%28%7Cy_i%20-%20%5Chat%7By%7D_i%7C%20-%20%5Cfrac%7B1%7D%7B2%7D%5Cdelta%29%2C%20%26%20%5Ctext%7Botherwise.%7D%20%5Cend%7Bcases%7D%20%5C%5C%20%5C%5C%20%5C%5C%20Huber%20%3D%20%5Cfrac%7B%20%5Csum_%7B%20i%20%3D%201%20%7D%20%5E%20%7B%20n%20%7D%20%28L_%7B%5Cdelta%7D%28y_i%2C%20%5Chat%7By%7D_i%29%29%20%7D%20%7Bn%7D)


* I would use `mae()` as a guide. 

- [ ] Call it `huber_loss()`

- [ ] It would require a `delta` argument for the cutoff value. The standard seems to be to default this to `1`. See `ccc()` to learn how to use optional arguments.

- [ ] Pay close attention to how we generate documentation and examples automatically

- [ ] Try and understand how `metric_summarizer()` works, along with the rationale behind `metric_vec_template()`, then use them in the implementation.

- [ ] Add a few tests. Small examples you can match from academic papers are best, but otherwise any online example is okay. If all else fails, create an example "by hand" that is easy to manually compute the result for.

- [ ] Use the file naming scheme `num-<metric>.R`

If you take on this metric, I would also encourage you to implement the Pseudo-Huber loss function if you have time (maybe do a separate Pull Request for it). It is on the same page as the huber loss, just scroll down. I would call it `huber_loss_pseudo()`.

- [ ] In the `seealso` section of the docs, cross link to `huber_loss()`

Tensorflow defines this metric:
https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/losses/huber_loss

The [Custom Metrics](https://tidymodels.github.io/yardstick/articles/custom-metrics.html) vignette will probably be helpful.

title: Mean Absolute Scaled Error (MASE)
description:
Definition:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mean_absolute_scaled_error

See also the Scale Free Errors section of:
http://datascienceassn.org/sites/default/files/Another%20Look%20at%20Measures%20of%20Forecast%20Accuracy.pdf


- I would use `mape()` as a general guide.
- There is a seasonal and non-seasonal version. The non-seasonal version is just the seasonal version with `m = 1` so we can just implement 1 version that handles seasonality and defaults to the non-seasonal version.
- To see how extra arguments can be passed through, use `ccc()` as a guide. Specifically, you need to pass it through in the `metric_summarizer()` and in the metric_vec_template()`.

- [ ] Call it `mase()`

- [ ] Because of the seasonality, it will need a parameter to control that. I would call it `period = 1` and document clearly that this controls the seasonal period in the calculation. (this is `m` in the wiki documentation)

- [ ] Pay close attention to how we generate documentation and examples automatically

- [ ] Try and understand how `metric_summarizer()` works, along with the rationale behind `metric_vec_template()`, then use them in the implementation.

- [ ] Add a few tests. Small examples you can match from academic papers are best, but otherwise any online example is okay. If all else fails, create an example "by hand" that is easy to manually compute the result for.

- [ ] Use the file naming scheme `num-<metric>.R`

- [ ] I would use add a documentation reference to the paper by Hyndman, since it is a metric he helped develop http://datascienceassn.org/sites/default/files/Another%20Look%20at%20Measures%20of%20Forecast%20Accuracy.pdf

The [Custom Metrics](https://tidymodels.github.io/yardstick/articles/custom-metrics.html) vignette will probably be helpful.

title: F-measure functions fail when precision or recall is undefined
description:
Example:
``` r
library(yardstick)
#> For binary classification, the first factor level is assumed to be the event.
#> Set the global option `yardstick.event_first` to `FALSE` to change this.

# Prepare data
truth    <- factor(c(rep("a", 10), rep("b", 2)))
estimate <- factor(rep("b", length(truth)), levels(truth))

# Calculate F-measure
f_meas_vec(truth, estimate)
#> Error in if (precision == 0 & rec == 0) {: missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed
f_meas(data.frame(truth, estimate), truth, estimate)
#> Error in summarise_impl(.data, dots): Evaluation error: missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed.
```

<sup>Created on 2019-01-22 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.1)</sup>

I think the issue lies in `yardstick:::f_meas_binary()`. This function checks whether precision and recall are zero so that it can return zero early before the actual F-measure calculation. However, the precision and recall values calculated by `yardstick:::precision_binary()` and `yardstick:::recall_binary()` can return NA if the denominator in the respective calculations is zero. If either returns NA then the logical check in `yardstick:::f_meas_binary()` can't be evaluated and returns an error.

title: mcc NAs produced by integer overflow
description:
In the case of large enough samples (`n`=200000) in this example, `mcc` will produce a warning message:
> 1 mcc     binary            NA
> Warning messages:
> 1: In tp * tn : NAs produced by integer overflow
> 2: In fp * fn : NAs produced by integer overflow

I believe this can be solved by rewriting the equation for `mcc` in a way to avoid the overflow at the cost of additional operations, but also can be handled in a quick and dirty way of changing the types of `tp`, `tn`, `fp`, and  `fn` from `integer` to `double`:
```r
tp <- as.double(tp)
tn <- as.double(tn)
fp <- as.double(fp)
fn <- as.double(fn)
```
which gives the answer
>1 mcc     binary      0.000267

I can submit a pull request on this simple hack if you think it will help.

```r
library(data.table)

n <- 100000
set.seed(808)
facs <- c("Class1", "Class2")
dt <- data.table(prob_1 = runif(n),
                 Class = sample(facs, size = n, replace = TRUE))
dt[, pred := factor(ifelse(prob_1 > 0.5, "Class1", "Class2"), levels = facs)]
dt[, Class := factor(Class, levels = facs)]
dt

library(yardstick)
conf_mat(dt, truth = Class, estimate = pred)
mcc(data = dt, truth = Class, estimate = pred)

n <- 200000
set.seed(808)
facs <- c("Class1", "Class2")
dt <- data.table(prob_1 = runif(n),
                 Class = sample(facs, size = n, replace = TRUE))
dt[, pred := factor(ifelse(prob_1 > 0.5, "Class1", "Class2"), levels = facs)]
dt[, Class := factor(Class, levels = facs)]
dt

library(yardstick)
conf_mat(dt, truth = Class, estimate = pred)
mcc(data = dt, truth = Class, estimate = pred)
```

https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/7b136e9/sklearn/metrics/ranking.py#L226

title: `metrics()` default value for `na.rm`
description: This currently defaults to `TRUE`, which means `NA`s in the prediction will be silently ignored. This could be potentially dangerous since the users may think their prediction functions are behaving normally upon seeing reasonable metrics. (Here I'm subjectively claiming that `NA` prediction outputs are "abnormal"...) Are there modeling applications where `NA` predictions are expected? If they're not the norm could we consider displaying a warning if `na.rm` isn't set by the user or changing the default?

title: make rsq() metrics tolerant to constant predictions
description:
``` r
library(yardstick)
#> For binary classification, the first factor level is assumed to be the event.
#> Set the global option `yardstick.event_first` to `FALSE` to change this.

set.seed(13)
dat <- tibble::tibble(obs = rnorm(20), pred = 1)
rsq(dat, truth = obs, estimate = pred)
#> Warning in cor(truth, estimate): the standard deviation is zero
#> # A tibble: 1 x 3
#>   .metric .estimator .estimate
#>   <chr>   <chr>          <dbl>
#> 1 rsq     standard          NA
```

<sup>Created on 2019-08-12 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.1)</sup>

I propose that we silently return zero:

```r
rsq_impl <- function(truth, estimate) {
  if (length(unique(estimate)) == 1) {
    return(0)
  }
  cor(truth, estimate)^2
}
```

At the minimum, a better warning should be issued.

title: mean log loss when true class has 0 probability
description:
The `mn_log_loss()` function doesn't seem to implement the [min max rule](http://wiki.fast.ai/index.php/Log_Loss#MinMax_Rule) as was done in `MLmetrics::MultiLogLoss()`. Thus, there is no penalization for really poor predictions where the true class had a class probability of 0.
``` r
# Example from MLmetrics::MultiLogLoss()
data(iris)
svm.model <- e1071::svm(Species ~ ., data = iris, probability = TRUE)
pred <- predict(svm.model, iris, probability = TRUE)
prob <- attr(pred, "probabilities")

# There is no difference when the truth has a non-zero probability
MLmetrics::MultiLogLoss(y_true = iris$Species, y_pred = prob)
#> [1] 0.07835234
yardstick::mn_log_loss_vec(truth = iris$Species, estimate = prob)
#> [1] 0.07835234

# Different handling of log loss when the truth has zero probability
iris$Species[1]
#> [1] setosa
#> Levels: setosa versicolor virginica
prob[1, ]
#>      setosa  versicolor   virginica 
#> 0.980533866 0.010535699 0.008930435
prob2 <- prob
prob2[1, ] <-  c(0, 0.5, 0.5)
MLmetrics::MultiLogLoss(y_true = iris$Species, y_pred = prob2)
#> [1] 0.3084798
yardstick::mn_log_loss_vec(truth = iris$Species, estimate = prob2)
#> [1] 0.07822128

# Set parameters to mn_log_loss_multiclass
truth <- iris$Species
estimate <- prob2
sum <- FALSE

# Use modified pos_log() with epsilon
y <- model.matrix(~truth - 1)
res <- y * estimate
res[res <= .Machine$double.eps & res > 0] <- .Machine$double.eps
pos_log <- function(x) {
  if (all(x == 0)) {
    log(1e-15)
  } else {
    log(x[x != 0])
  }
}
  res <- -sum(unlist(apply(res, 1, pos_log)))
if (!sum) 
  res <- res/length(truth)
res
#> [1] 0.3084798
```

title: New metric: AUNU
description:
> AUC of each class against the rest, using the uniform class distribution.

I believe this is equivalent to ROC AUC with `estimator = "macro"`, but I have seen this metric used by itself in a number of places, so it would probably be good to include it as a standalone version.

Reference: 
Page 30 of:
https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~saito/data/roc/ferri-class-perf-metrics.pdf

Essentially, this would create a wrapper around `roc_auc_vec(estimator = "macro")`.

If you tackle this issue, it would be great if you could:

- Use `roc_auc()` as a general guide for the structure.

- [ ] First ensure that I am correct in understanding that this is the same as `roc_auc(estimator = "macro")`. Perhaps go out and find another package that implements this metric and check the results of a small example (that's what I would probably do).

- [ ] Call it `roc_aunu()`.

- [ ] Pay close attention to how we generate documentation and examples automatically

- [ ] Try and understand how `metric_summarizer()` works, along with the rationale behind `metric_vec_template()`, then use them in the implementation.

- [ ] Add a few tests. Small examples you can match from academic papers are best, but otherwise any online example is okay. If all else fails, create an example "by hand" that is easy to manually compute the result for.

- [ ] Use the file naming scheme `prob-<metric>.R`

- [ ] No `estimator` argument would be required for this function. Please document that it is the same as macro averaged `roc_auc()`.

- [ ] Please add a reference section to the linked paper.

The `roc_aunu_impl()` function will probably just call `roc_auc_vec(truth, estimate, options, estimator = "macro", na_rm = FALSE, ...)` (`na_rm = FALSE` because it would already have been taken care of)

The [Custom Metrics](https://tidymodels.github.io/yardstick/articles/custom-metrics.html) vignette will probably be helpful.

title: Store event_first in conf_mat objects
description:
Currently, for binary classification, it seems that whether or not the event is the first factor level can only be set globally, via `options(yardstick.event_first = FALSE)`.

Semantically, it feels as though the event level ought to be a property of the confusion matrix. By storing the event column in the `conf_mat` object, you can more easily work with a mix of response types where sometimes the event is the first level, and other times it is not.

### Minimal, reproducible example:

First, we define two confusion matrices, one where the event isn't the first value, and another where it is.

``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(yardstick)
#> For binary classification, the first factor level is assumed to be the event.
#> Set the global option `yardstick.event_first` to `FALSE` to change this.
library(withr)

actual_response1 <- rep(c(0, 1, 0, 1), 1:4)
predicted_response1 <- rep(c(0, 0, 1, 1), 1:4)
outcomes1 <- table(predicted_response1, actual_response1)
(confusion1 <- conf_mat(outcomes1))
#>                    actual_response1
#> predicted_response1 0 1
#>                   0 1 2
#>                   1 3 4

actual_response2 <- factor(rep(c("neg", "pos", "neg", "pos"), 1:4), levels = c("pos", "neg"))
predicted_response2 <- factor(rep(c("neg", "neg", "pos", "pos"), 1:4), levels = c("pos", "neg"))
outcomes2 <- table(predicted_response2, actual_response2)
(confusion2 <- conf_mat(outcomes2))
#>                    actual_response2
#> predicted_response2 pos neg
#>                 pos   4   3
#>                 neg   2   1
```

Now if you want to calculate performance metrics, you have to write grim code that specifies a global option.

```r
with_options(
  c(yardstick.event_first = FALSE),
  summary(confusion1)
)
#> # A tibble: 13 x 3
#>    .metric              .estimator .estimate
#>    <chr>                <chr>          <dbl>
#>  1 accuracy             binary        0.5   
#>  2 kap                  binary       -0.0870
#>  3 sens                 binary        0.667 
#>  4 spec                 binary        0.25  
#>  5 ppv                  binary        0.571 
#>  6 npv                  binary        0.333 
#>  7 mcc                  binary       -0.0891
#>  8 j_index              binary       -0.0833
#>  9 bal_accuracy         binary        0.458 
#> 10 detection_prevalence binary        0.7   
#> 11 precision            binary        0.571 
#> 12 recall               binary        0.667 
#> 13 f_meas               binary        0.615

with_options(
  c(yardstick.event_first = TRUE),
  summary(confusion2)
)
#> # A tibble: 13 x 3
#>    .metric              .estimator .estimate
#>    <chr>                <chr>          <dbl>
#>  1 accuracy             binary        0.5   
#>  2 kap                  binary       -0.0870
#>  3 sens                 binary        0.667 
#>  4 spec                 binary        0.25  
#>  5 ppv                  binary        0.571 
#>  6 npv                  binary        0.333 
#>  7 mcc                  binary       -0.0891
#>  8 j_index              binary       -0.0833
#>  9 bal_accuracy         binary        0.458 
#> 10 detection_prevalence binary        0.7   
#> 11 precision            binary        0.571 
#> 12 recall               binary        0.667 
#> 13 f_meas               binary        0.615
```

### Possible changes to `conf_mat()`

I suggest that `conf_mat()` should gain an extra argument, like

```r
first_event = getOption("yardstick.first_event", TRUE)
```

There are several possibilities for how to store the first event information in a `conf_mat` object.

1. Store a logical first event value

In `conf_mat.table()`, the confusion matrix object would be stored as

```r
structure(
    list(table = data, first_event = first_event, dots = list(...)),
    class = "conf_mat"
  )
```

2. Store the column number for the event

Here, you'd calculate the position from the first event argument.

```r
event_col_posn = if(first_event) 1 else 2

structure(
    list(table = data, event_col_posn = event_col_posn, dots = list(...)),
    class = "conf_mat"
  )
```

3. Store the column name for the event

This is similar to the last idea, but stores the name rather than the position.

```r
event_col_posn = if(first_event) 1 else 2
event_col_name = names(dimnames(data))[event_col_posn]

structure(
    list(table = data, event_col_name = event_col_name, dots = list(...)),
    class = "conf_mat"
  )
```

## Ramifications

1. This takes precedence anywhere ` getOption("yardstick.first_event") appears

The global option is currently used in a few places, notably `pos_val()` and `neg_val()`. These functions would need to be modified to receive the value from the confusion matrix.

2. It's not clear how to deal with cases of more than two response categories

I've been concentrating on binary classification. Where there are more than two responses, it isn't totally clear what the behavior ought to be, since there isn't a single "event" category. I don't see any harm in storing the `first_event` value (or whichever you decide on) as `NA`. You probably need to think this through properly though.

title: collect_metrics(), pr_auc() and MLmetrics::PRAUC() all give different results on the same data
description:
I'm training a model using `tune::tune_grid()` with `metrics = yardstick::metric_set(pr_auc)`. On my data `collect_metrics()` always comes back as `0.99` (tiny 0.00000xx variations) for every fold/parameter combination, but then `pr_auc` calculates a much saner value. `MLmetrics::PRAUC()` calculates yet another value. This shouldn't be the case especially after `last_fit`, because the data never changes.

Here's a reprex. I set `options(yardstick.event_first = FALSE)` because in this data I want to predict the "pos" class, which is the second level.
