``` r
data("PimaIndiansDiabetes2")
options(yardstick.event_first = FALSE) 

set.seed(73487)

xgb_split <- rsample::initial_split(PimaIndiansDiabetes2, strata = diabetes, prop = 0.7)
xgb_train <- rsample::training(xgb_split)
xgb_test <- rsample::testing(xgb_split)

xgb_recipe <- recipe(diabetes ~ ., data = xgb_train)

xgb_model <- parsnip::boost_tree(
  trees = 50, 
  tree_depth = tune::tune(), min_n = tune::tune(),
  loss_reduction = tune::tune(),
  sample_size = tune::tune(), mtry = tune::tune(),
  learn_rate = tune::tune(),
) %>% 
  parsnip::set_engine("xgboost") %>% 
  parsnip::set_mode("classification")


xgb_grid <- dials::grid_max_entropy(
  dials::min_n(),
  dials::tree_depth(c(3, 10)),
  dials::loss_reduction(),
  sample_size = dials::sample_prop(c(0.5, 1)),
  dials::finalize(dials::mtry(), recipes::prep(xgb_recipe) %>% recipes::juice()),
  dials::learn_rate(c(0.01, 0.3), trans = NULL),
  size = 7
)

xgb_workflow <- workflows::workflow() %>%
  workflows::add_model(., xgb_model) %>%
  workflows::add_recipe(., xgb_recipe)

cv_folds <- rsample::vfold_cv(
  xgb_train,
  strata = diabetes,
  v = 3
)

xgb_tuned_fit <- tune::tune_grid(
  xgb_workflow,
  resamples = cv_folds,
  grid = xgb_grid,
  metrics = yardstick::metric_set(pr_auc)
)
#> i Creating pre-processing data to finalize unknown parameter: mtry

max(tune::collect_metrics(xgb_tuned_fit)$mean)
#> [1] 0.6747191

best_model_params <- tune::select_best(xgb_tuned_fit, "pr_auc")

final_xgb <- tune::finalize_workflow(
  xgb_workflow,
  best_model_params
)

final_res <- tune::last_fit(
  final_xgb, 
  xgb_split,
  metrics = yardstick::metric_set(pr_auc))

tune::collect_metrics(final_res)$.estimate
#> [1] 0.2223544
preds <- collect_predictions(final_res) %>% 
  mutate(diabetes = as.factor(ifelse(diabetes == "pos", 1, 0)))
yardstick::pr_auc(preds, truth = diabetes, .pred_pos)$.estimate
#> [1] 0.6350597
MLmetrics::PRAUC(preds$.pred_pos, preds$diabetes)
#> [1] 0.6225597

#### if we switch the probs we get the same AUC from collect_metrics
#### but I explicitly yardstick.event_first = FALSE, meaning it's predicting "pos"
MLmetrics::PRAUC(preds$.pred_neg, preds$diabetes)
#> [1] 0.2223544
```

I created a new metric following the example:

```
scor_vec <- function(truth, estimate, na_rm = TRUE, ...) {
  scor_impl <- function(truth, estimate) {
    cor(truth, estimate, method='spearman')
  }
  metric_vec_template(
    metric_impl = scor_impl,
    truth = truth, 
    estimate = estimate,
    na_rm = na_rm,
    cls = "numeric",
    ...
  )
  }

scor <- function(data, ...) {
  UseMethod("scor")
}

scor.data.frame <- function(data, truth, estimate, na_rm = TRUE, ...) {
  metric_summarizer(
    metric_nm = "scor",
    metric_fn = scor_vec,
    data = data,
    truth = !! enquo(truth),
    estimate = !! enquo(estimate), 
    na_rm = na_rm,
    ...
  )
}

class(scor) <- c("numeric_metric", class(scor))

```

title: A correlation computation is required, but `estimate` is constant and has 0 standard deviation, resulting in a divide by 0 error. `NA` will be returned.
description:
## The problem

When doing grid search in parameter tuning, the following message is returned:

```
A correlation computation is required, but `estimate` is constant and has 0 standard deviation, resulting in a divide by 0 error. `NA` will be returned.
```

There is not much documentation on it; the only mentions of it are in GitHub issues at tidymodels/tune#37 and tidymodels/yardstick#116, I believe.

This is particularly puzzling for me when using `glmnet` for performing LASSO regression.

## Reproducible example

Copy your code to the clipboard and run:

```r
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(glmnet)
n <- 5000
dat <- tibble(
  x1 = rnorm(n),
  x2 = rnorm(n),
  x3 = rnorm(n),
  x4 = rnorm(n),
  x5 = rnorm(n),
  y = x1 + rnorm(n)
)
wf <- workflow()

# split test and train ---------------------------------------------------------
set.seed(1839)
dat_split <- dat %>% 
  initial_split()

dat_train <- training(dat_split)
dat_test <- testing(dat_split)

# preprocessing ----------------------------------------------------------------
dat_train_prep <- recipe(y ~ ., data = dat_train) %>% 
  step_normalize(all_numeric())

wf <- wf %>% 
  add_recipe(dat_train_prep)

# specify model ----------------------------------------------------------------
lasso_spec <- linear_reg(penalty = tune(), mixture = 1) %>% 
  set_engine("glmnet")

wf <- wf %>% 
  add_model(lasso_spec)

# tune for lambda --------------------------------------------------------------
lasso_grid <- tune_grid(
  wf,
  resamples = vfold_cv(dat_train, v = 5),
  grid = grid_regular(penalty(), levels = 50)
)
```

To me, there should not be any places where a singular prediction is being made—that's not how I simulated the data or fit the model. I _think_ this might be happening because `glmnet` is performing `cv.glmnet` under the hood, which fits an intercept-only model first (_I think_), which would give a constant prediction.

Nevertheless, `glmnet` is a popular library, so if this happens in a simple example, I was thinking it might be worth documenting.

title: autoplot(type = "heatmap") fails on table with named dimensions
description:
If you are filing a bug, make sure these boxes are checked before submitting your issue— thank you!

- [x] Start a new R session
- [x] Install the latest version of of the package: `update.packages(oldPkgs="yardstick", ask=FALSE)`
- [x] [Write a minimal reproducible example](http://stackoverflow.com/a/5963610)
- [x] run `sessionInfo()` and add the results to the issue. Even better would be to use the [`sessioninfo`](https://github.com/r-lib/sessioninfo) package's `session_info()`.  

### Minimal, reproducible example:

1. Use `conf_mat()` to create a confusion matrix from a `base::table()` object.
2. Call `autoplot()` with `type = "heatmap"`.



#### Minimal, runnable code:

```r
library(ggplot2)
library(yardstick)
actual_response <- sample(0:1, 20, replace = TRUE)
predicted_response <- sample(0:1, 20, replace = TRUE)
outcomes <- table(predicted_response, actual_response)
confusion <- conf_mat(outcomes)

autoplot(confusion, type = "heatmap")
#> Error in factor(Prediction, levels = rev(levels(Prediction))): object 'Prediction' not found
```

The problem appears to originate in `cm_heat()`, [here](https://github.com/tidymodels/yardstick/blob/master/R/conf_mat.R#L315-L316).

The function assumes that the names of the columns in the data frame are always "Truth", "Prediction", and "Freq". The first two are actually the dimension names of the table.

description:
- [x] Start a new R session
- [x] Install the latest version of of the package: `update.packages(oldPkgs="yardstick", ask=FALSE)`
- [x] [Write a minimal reproducible example](http://stackoverflow.com/a/5963610)
- [x] run `sessionInfo()` and add the results to the issue. Even better would be to use the [`sessioninfo`](https://github.com/r-lib/sessioninfo) package's `session_info()`.  

### Minimal, reproducible example:

1. Create a confusion matrix.
2. Call `autoplot()` with the default `type = "mosaic"`.

#### Minimal, runnable code:

``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(yardstick)

actual_response <- rep(c(0, 1, 0, 1), 1:4)
predicted_response <- rep(c(0, 0, 1, 1), 1:4)
outcomes <- table(predicted_response, actual_response)
(confusion <- conf_mat(outcomes))
#>                   actual_response
#> predicted_response 0 1
#>                  0 1 2
#>                  1 3 4


autoplot(confusion)
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/nOBPDgu.png)

Since there are 4 actual responses of 0 and 6 actual responses of 1, I expected the widths of the columns to be a 40-60 split. They are actually a 30-70 split.

It looks like the problem is the use of `rowSums()` instead of `colSums()`, [here](https://github.com/tidymodels/yardstick/blob/master/R/conf_mat.R#L352).

For comparison, here's the equivalent plot using `vcd::mosaic()`.

``` r
library(vcd)
actual_response <- rep(c(0, 1, 0, 1), 1:4)
predicted_response <- rep(c(0, 0, 1, 1), 1:4)
mosaic(~ actual_response + predicted_response, direction = c("v", "h"))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/36NIgjW.png)

You can see the column width split is different here.

title: Class metric sets require named arguments while numeric metric sets accept positional matches
description:
Hi,

Just wondering why you have to specify `truth = ...` and `estimate = ...` for the class-based metric sets  as shown below, but not for the numeric based metrics. Maybe its something obvious I'm not seeing.
``` r
library(tidyverse)
library(yardstick)

# Class-based metric set
ms <- metric_set(accuracy, mcc)

iris %>% 
  ms(Species, Species)
```

title: Resampled metrics wrong when `yardstick.event_first = FALSE`
description:
Hi!

#133  The problem

I'm having trouble with resampling and collecting metrics (especially ROC-AUC) from a `glm` model. When using `yes` as the positive and first level for the outcome of a classification problem, the coefficients have the wrong sign (I think because `glm` uses the first level as reference level), but the resampled and manually calculated metrics are the same and correct (see below).
When using `no` as the first level and setting `yardstick.event_first = FALSE`, the coefficients are correct, but the resampled metrics are wrong. The predictions and manually calculated metrics are correct, though.

## Reproducible example

``` r
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)

set.seed(123)

data("titanic_imputed", package = "DALEX")

options(yardstick.event_first = TRUE)

titanic_data_yesfirst <-
  titanic_imputed %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  mutate(survived = factor(survived, levels = c("1", "0"), labels = c("yes", "no")))

training_folds_yesfirst <-
  vfold_cv(titanic_data_yesfirst, v = 10, repeats = 2, strata = survived)

model.glm <-
  logistic_reg() %>%
  set_engine("glm")

workflow.glm <-
  workflow() %>%
  add_formula(survived ~ .) %>%
  add_model(model.glm)

fit.glm_yesfirst <-
  workflow.glm %>%
  fit(data = titanic_data_yesfirst)

resamples.glm_yesfirst <-
  workflow.glm %>%
  fit_resamples(
    training_folds_yesfirst,
    metrics = metric_set(accuracy, roc_auc),
    control = control_resamples(
      save_pred = TRUE
      )
    )
#> ! Fold01, Repeat1: internal: The `yardstick.event_first` option has been deprecated as of y...

summary(fit.glm_yesfirst %>%
          pull_workflow_fit() %>% .$fit)

  workflow.glm %>%
  fit(data = titanic_data_nofirst)

  workflow.glm %>%
  fit_resamples(
    training_folds_nofirst,
    metrics = metric_set(accuracy, roc_auc),
    control = control_resamples(
      save_pred = TRUE
    )
  )
```

title: Access to class components used in macro averaging
description:
When developing multi class models it's often necessary to explore the fit for each class. One reason is that a few key classes may be more important to get right than the rest, so we want to ensure they are being fit well. 

Given that macro averaging actually calculates each classes metric would it be possible for these components to also be added to the returned object so, if necessary, people can assess each class? 

I think it would help alot of people, some papers seem to expect these class specific metrics.

title: Metric: Add metrics that rely on log-likelihood calculation
description: Popular metrics such as [Akaike Information Criterion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akaike_information_criterion), [Bayesian Information Criterion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayesian_information_criterion), or [Hannan-Quinn information criterion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannan-Quinn_information_criterion) require additional information on the fitted model in order to be computed, such as log-likelihood or number of observations. Could they be added within `yardstick`?

title: Confidence intervals do not work for roc_auc
description:
## The problem

The `ci` argument to `pROC::roc()` doesn't get used when passed to `yardstick::roc_auc()`. Other arguments do work. Any particular reason why this is the case? I couldn't find anything in the documentation about this.

``` r
library(magrittr)
```

``` r
# Summary metrics of trained models -----------------------------------------
custom_summary <- function (data, lev = NULL,  model = NULL) {
  if(length(unique(data$pred)) < 2 || length(unique(data$obs)) < 2)  {    
    resamplCor <- NA  } else {    resamplCor <- try(cor(data$pred, data$obs, use = "pairwise.complete.obs"), silent = TRUE)
    if (inherits(resamplCor, "try-error")) resamplCor <- NA  }
  rmse <- hydroGOF::rmse(sim = data$pred, obs = data$obs, na.rm=TRUE)
  nrmse <- hydroGOF::nrmse(sim = data$pred, obs = data$obs, norm = "maxmin", na.rm=TRUE)
  pred_error <- (data$obs - data$pred)
  apz <- 100*(length(which(pred_error > -1 & pred_error < 0.5))/length(pred_error))
  out <- c(nrmse, resamplCor^2, apz, rmse)
  names(out) <- c("NRMSE", "Rsquared", "APZ", "RMSE")
  out
}
```

title: Plotting the summary statistics of a confusion matrix
description:
Both `summary.conf_mat` and `autoplot.conf_mat` are attempts to explain a confusion matrix. However, I thought one could plot the summary statistics on the margins of the confusion matrix as an additional way for explaining the summary statistics and ultimately the confusion matrix itself. For instance, it could be hard to explain to a layman what is the difference between the "positive predictive value" and the "true positive rate".

My attempt, available as a [forked repo](https://github.com/kevinwang09/yardstick) follows from [this Wikipedia table](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sensitivity_and_specificity#Confusion_matrix). Some key features are:

+ This only works with a binary class example. 
+ Similar to the existing `heatmap` option, the raw counts of events are shown, but with an additional percentage calculation. 
+ Each of the marginal tables is generated as a separate ggplot and pasted together using `patchwork`. 
+ The fill colour ranges from blue to white to yellow, with blue colours implying a favourable result and yellow implying an unfavourable result. The blue and yellow were chosen to suit colour-vision-deficient individuals. 

I am keen to hear your thoughts on this extension and if there is an interest for this to be incorporated as a pull request. 

Thanks. Kevin.

title: pROC::roc and yardstick::roc_auc have opposite results when specifying same direction
description:
Hi,

It seems like the `direction` argument when passed directly to `pROC::roc()` operates in the opposite way as when it is passed in a list of options via `options` to `yardstick::roc_auc()`. I have simulated some data below which explicitly have made the "cases" group have a higher predictort value than the "controls" group.

According to the help documentation for `pROC::roc()`, here is the descrition of how to use the direction argument:

> in which direction to make the comparison? “auto” (default): automatically define in which group the median is higher and take the direction accordingly. “>”: if the predictor values for the control group are higher than the values of the case group (controls > t >= cases). “<”: if the predictor values for the control group are lower or equal than the values of the case group (controls < t <= cases). You should set this explicity to “>” or “<” whenever you are resampling or randomizing the data, otherwise the curves will be biased towards higher AUC values.

Based on this description, I would set `direction = "<"`, since controls have lower predictor values. When I do this in `pROC::roc()` directly, I get the correct AUC and it agrees with the "auto" method. However, when passed as an option to `yardstick::roc_auc()` I get the complementary AUC. When flipping the direction to `">"` for `roc_auc()` it now agrees with `"<"` for `roc()`.

I can't tell if I am losing my mind or if this an actual bug.

``` r
library(dplyr)

set.seed(1234)
data <-
  tibble(
    bi = rep(c(0L, 1L), each = 20),
    pr = c(rnorm(20, -1), rnorm(20, 1))
  ) %>% 
  mutate(bi = factor(bi, levels = c(0, 1)))

data %>% group_by(bi) %>% summarise(median(pr))
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>   bi    `median(pr)`
#>   <fct>        <dbl>
#> 1 0           -1.53 
#> 2 1            0.504

data %>% 
  pROC::roc(bi, pr)
#> Setting levels: control = 0, case = 1
#> Setting direction: controls < cases
#> 
#> Call:
#> roc.data.frame(data = ., response = bi, predictor = pr)
#> 
#> Data: pr in 20 controls (bi 0) < 20 cases (bi 1).
#> Area under the curve: 0.91

data %>% 
  pROC::roc(bi, pr, direction = '<')
#> Setting levels: control = 0, case = 1
#> 
#> Call:
#> roc.data.frame(data = ., response = bi, predictor = pr, direction = "<")
#> 
#> Data: pr in 20 controls (bi 0) < 20 cases (bi 1).
#> Area under the curve: 0.91

data %>% 
  pROC::roc(bi, pr, direction = '>')
#> Setting levels: control = 0, case = 1
#> 
#> Call:
#> roc.data.frame(data = ., response = bi, predictor = pr, direction = ">")
#> 
#> Data: pr in 20 controls (bi 0) > 20 cases (bi 1).
#> Area under the curve: 0.09

data %>% 
  yardstick::roc_auc(bi, pr)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 3
#>   .metric .estimator .estimate
#>   <chr>   <chr>          <dbl>
#> 1 roc_auc binary         0.910

data %>% 
  yardstick::roc_auc(bi, pr, options = list(direction = '<'))
#> # A tibble: 1 x 3
#>   .metric .estimator .estimate
#>   <chr>   <chr>          <dbl>
#> 1 roc_auc binary          0.09

data %>% 
  yardstick::roc_auc(bi, pr, options = list(direction = '>'))
#> # A tibble: 1 x 3
#>   .metric .estimator .estimate
#>   <chr>   <chr>          <dbl>
#> 1 roc_auc binary         0.910
```

title: Calibratrion metrics x Discriminant metrics
description:
### Calibration Metrics in Tidymodels

 I would like to request calibration metrics to yardstick as https://github.com/tidymodels/yardstick/issues/150

I fitted a model using tidymodels and select the best model by 10-fold-cross validation and test the accuracy with roc_auc and confusion matrix. This model was submitted to publication and the reviewers request the calibration metrics. I perform these calibration metrics using the RMS package. I had a disagreement in Elastic Net between discriminant metrics (roc_auc, sensibility, and specificity) and calibration metrics (Brier Score and slope values).

Can anyone help me with this divergence between calibration and discrimination measures? Was the model trained using measures of discrimination (roc_auc) and not calibration justifying the difference? Which measure is most relevant?
